title: Install and maintain irrigation filtration systems

lessons.title: Filtration requirements for irrigation
lessons.html:
Why filtration matters

Drippers, micro-sprayers and small sprinkler nozzles have tiny passages. Sand, silt, algae, organic debris, insect larvae and chemical precipitates block them, causing dry spots, uneven growth and expensive replacement. Filtration removes these particles before they enter the system. The finer the emitter passages, the finer the filtration needed.

Matching filter to water source

Water sourceTypical contaminantsSuitable filtration
Municipal waterLow load; occasional pipe scale or sand after repairsScreen or disc filter
BoreholeSand, iron and manganese precipitatesSand separator (hydrocyclone) followed by screen or disc
Dam, river, canalAlgae, organic matter, silt, larvaeSand (media) filters followed by disc or screen
Recycled or effluent waterHigh organic loadMedia filters, often with chemical treatment

Filter types

  • Screen filters: a stainless steel or plastic mesh. Good for hard particles like sand; clog quickly with algae.
  • Disc filters: stacks of grooved plastic discs; trap particles in depth, good for organic matter and easy to backflush.
  • Sand (media) filters: tanks filled with graded silica sand or crushed media; best for heavy organic loads such as dam water.
  • Hydrocyclones (sand separators): spin water to throw heavy sand out; no use for light organic matter.

Filtration grade

Filtration grade is expressed in micron or mesh. The emitter manufacturer states the required filtration for its product; follow it. A finer filter than necessary causes higher pressure loss and more frequent cleaning.

Pressure loss

A clean filter causes a small pressure loss. As it clogs, the loss increases. Pressure gauges before and after the filter show the differential pressure; when it reaches the value set by the manufacturer, the filter must be cleaned or backflushed. Size filters for the system flow so the clean pressure loss stays low.

lessons.title: Installing self-flushing screen and disc filter banks
lessons.html:
Planning the installation

Self-flushing filter banks use several filter units connected by an inlet manifold and an outlet manifold. When one unit is flushed, the others keep filtering, so irrigation continues.

  1. Check the design: number and size of filters, manifold diameters, flow rate, and the position on the delivery pipeline (after the pump and fertiliser injection point, before the mainline).
  2. Prepare a level concrete plinth or firm base with enough space around it for servicing, and a drain route for flush water away from the pump house and electrical equipment.
  3. Check that the system pressure is enough for flushing; most automatic filters need a minimum pressure to flush effectively. If not, a pressure-sustaining valve downstream may be required.

Assembling the manifolds

  • Lay out the inlet and outlet manifolds (PVC, HDPE or steel, as specified) with flanged or grooved couplings to each filter.
  • Fit the flush valve of each unit to a common flush manifold discharging to the drain.
  • Install isolating valves at the inlet and outlet of the bank so it can be bypassed or serviced.
  • Install pressure gauges or pressure tapping points before and after the bank for differential pressure readings.
  • Fit an air release valve on the high point of the outlet manifold.
  • Support manifolds so the weight of pipe and water does not hang on the filter bodies.

Commissioning

  1. Flush the pipeline before connecting so construction debris does not reach the filters.
  2. Pressurise slowly, with air release open, and check all joints for leaks.
  3. Record clean differential pressure at design flow.
  4. Run a manual flush on each unit and check that flush water discharges and the unit returns to filtering.

Safety

Never open a filter housing or clamp under pressure; isolate and release pressure first. Lift heavy filter bodies with two people or a hoist. Electrical connections to the control unit are for qualified electricians.

lessons.title: Sand filter systems, automatic controls and maintenance
lessons.html:
Assembling a self-flushing sand filter system

  1. Place the tanks on a level plinth in a row, with the spacing that the manifolds require.
  2. Check internal parts: underdrain laterals or nozzles must be undamaged, as broken parts let sand into the irrigation system.
  3. Fill the tanks with the specified grade and depth of filter media, adding water first to cushion the underdrain. Leave the freeboard (space above the sand) the manufacturer specifies so media can expand during backwash without being washed out.
  4. Connect the inlet manifold to the tops and the outlet manifold to the bottoms through three-way backwash valves.
  5. Connect the backwash outlets to a common drain manifold with a backwash flow control valve to stop media loss.
  6. Install a secondary screen or disc filter downstream of the sand filters to catch any media that escapes.

Automatic backwash controls

A backwash controller opens each tank's valve in turn, so clean water from the other tanks flows backwards through it, lifting the sand and flushing dirt to drain.

  • Triggers: a differential pressure switch (backwash when dirty), a timer (backwash at intervals), or both.
  • Settings: differential pressure set-point, time interval, flush duration per tank, and the dwell time between tanks, all from the manufacturer's guidance and adjusted for water quality.
  • Hydraulic command tubes from the controller to valves must be correctly connected and kept free of kinks.

Service and maintenance

TaskWhy
Record differential pressure daily or weeklyShows filter condition and controller performance
Check backwash water runs clear by the end of the cycleConfirms flush duration is enough
Inspect sand for clumping, channels, and loss of depthClumped media lets dirty water through
Top up or replace media as per manufacturerMedia wears and becomes rounded
Clean screens and discs manually when neededRemove stubborn algae or scale
Check seals, valves, gauges and controller batteriesPrevent leaks and missed cycles

Chemical cleaning of media (chlorine for organic matter, acid for scale) is done only under supervision, following the product label and with full PPE.

Key points

  • Choose filtration to suit the water source and the emitter's requirements.
  • Install isolating valves, gauges and air release on filter banks.
  • Leave freeboard in sand filters and fit a secondary filter downstream.
  • Set backwash on differential pressure and time, and check flush water runs clear.
  • Never open filters under pressure.
